# R5 Digest — Provan, *1 and 2 Kings* (NIBC 1995), §35–§46

**Source:** Iain W. Provan, *1 and 2 Kings*, NIBC  
**Slice:** `R5_elisha_2535-3276.txt` (cache lines 1–742 ≈ raw 2535–3276)  
**Scope:** Moab/Mesha (2 Kgs 3); Elisha miracles (ch. 4); Naaman (ch. 5); axehead/Arameans (6:1–23); siege of Samaria (6:24–7:20); end-of-Ahab setup (ch. 8); Jehu (9–10); Athaliah/Joash (11); Joash temple repair (12); Jehoahaz/Jehoash + Elisha’s death/bones (13); **§46 Excursus: Elisha in Canonical Context**  
**Rules:** Extraction only; no live wiki edits. Claims attributed to Provan. Verbatim anchors + loci (slice line numbers).

---

### C-R5-01 — Jehoram distanced from Ahab’s Baal-worship but still judged
**Claim:** Provan reads Jehoram as surprisingly better than Ahab/Jezebel and Ahaziah: he removes Baal’s sacred stone and is not explicitly accused of Baal-worship in chs. 3–9, yet still “clings” to Jeroboam’s calves and is worthy of judgment; Baal-cult remains alive under his tolerance.
**Quote:** “It is surprising, then, to find that the description of his reign distances him from the rest of his family. He did evil . . . but not as his father and mother had done. … Jehoram is presented, then, as tolerating the Baal cult while not himself necessarily participating in it. … His sins are still, of course, worthy of divine judgment.”
**Locus:** §35; 2 Kgs 3:1–3; slice ll. 13
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-02 — Moab campaign deliberately echoes 1 Kgs 22; Jehoshaphat forgets the prophet
**Claim:** Provan holds that Jehoram’s alliance with Jehoshaphat deliberately recalls 1 Kgs 22, but this time Jehoshaphat skips consulting the LORD and goes straight to tactics—piety appears amiss until desert disaster restores the prophetic inquiry.
**Quote:** “Immediately, then, we are quite deliberately reminded of the earlier story and invited to make comparisons. … whereas, earlier, Jehoshaphat was very concerned to discover ‘the counsel of the LORD’ before going off to war (22:5), he now moves directly from agreement to tactics … There is no prophet in sight. … Something seems amiss.”
**Locus:** §35; 2 Kgs 3:4–12; slice ll. 15–17
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-03 — Elisha’s Moab oracle is partial truth, not falsehood; prophets do not control the word
**Claim:** On the surprise reverse at Kir Haresheth, Provan argues Elisha did not lie: everything predicted happened, but crucial end-information was withheld so wicked kings (and readers) expected total victory; God lures Jehoram via partial revelation through a true prophet. Central lesson: prophets are channels, not masters of the word; God need not give full disclosure.
**Quote:** “Elisha did not lie. There is in his prophecy, nevertheless, a certain economy with the truth. … Once again a wicked Israelite king has been lured to disaster, this time not by a lying spirit speaking through false prophets, but by the Spirit of God revealing partial truth to a true prophet. … A central lesson of the chapter is this: prophets do not control the prophetic word. … They are simply channels through which it passes. … God does not always reveal the entirety of the divine will, particularly when faced with wicked Israelite kings destined for judgment.”
**Locus:** §35; 2 Kgs 3:13–27; slice ll. 19–27
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-04 — “Fury” at Mesha’s child sacrifice is human (then divinely effective), not Chemosh or LORD accepting child sacrifice
**Claim:** Provan rejects reading *qeṣep* as Chemosh’s wrath (would grant real existence to a “detestable thing”) or as the LORD’s fury linked to acceptable child sacrifice. More likely first-instance human superhuman fury of Mesha’s troops; at another level the LORD still ordains the reverse for Israel.
**Quote:** “To argue, on the one hand, that the authors had in mind the wrath of the Moabite god Chemosh … is to ignore everything we have read up to this point about the LORD alone being God … To argue, on the other hand, that it is the LORD’s fury that is meant … is to accept that the authors are allowing for a link between child sacrifice and divine action … This, too, seems unlikely. It is much more likely that the fury is thought of as in the first instance human … The Moabites’ anger would have counted for nothing, had God not ordained that it should count for something.”
**Locus:** §35 Additional Notes, 3:27; slice ll. 63
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-05 — Elisha-story pattern: the powerless know God; kings are ignorant and arrogant
**Claim:** Across 2 Kgs 3–8 Provan sees a structural pattern: politically powerless figures (servant, maid, lepers) are open to what God does through Elisha; kings reveal ignorance and arrogance and refuse humble respect toward the prophet.
**Quote:** “It is a pronounced feature of the Elisha stories in 2 Kgs. 3–8 that it is characteristically the politically powerless who are in touch with and open to what God is doing through Elisha, while the powerful (especially the kings) reveal only ignorance and arrogance, refusing to adopt a humble and respectful attitude towards him.”
**Locus:** §35 Additional Notes, 3:11; slice ll. 53
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-06 — Widow’s oil and Shunammite son deliberately parallel Elijah’s Zarephath sequence
**Claim:** Provan reads 4:1–7 and 4:8–37 as remaking Elijah’s 1 Kgs 17 provision/death/resurrection pattern: oil multiplies for a prophetic widow; unexpected life (son given to aged hostess) yields unforeseen death, then restoration by Elisha’s personal presence after Gehazi fails.
**Quote:** “Like the widow of Zarephath (1 Kgs. 17:7–16), she possesses only a small amount of oil … As in the Elijah story, this small amount is transformed into an abundance … The major part of the chapter is taken up with a story reminiscent of the sequel to the ‘widow narrative’ of 1 Kings 17:7–16 … The same basic elements—miraculous provision; unexpected death; prophetic intervention and restoration to life—are woven into a quite different story.”
**Locus:** §36; 2 Kgs 4:1–37; slice ll. 87–89
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-07 — Elisha incomplete knowledge again; Shunammite accuses him of misleading promise
**Claim:** “The LORD has hidden it from me” (4:27) continues the ch. 3 theme: God is no vending machine of oracles. The woman’s “Don’t mislead your servant” implies Elisha’s blessing-oracle suggested she would see the child grow; he does not quibble pedantically but accepts responsibility.
**Quote:** “Elisha did not know this would happen … This is a most interesting statement in view of what has just occurred in 2 Kgs. 3, where Elisha’s knowledge of the future was similarly incomplete. God is not a vending machine that pours out oracles when primed with prophetic pennies. … The implication of Elisha’s words in v. 16 was not only that she would see a child born but also that she would see that child grow up. Now she is here to accuse him of deceit. Elisha does not take refuge in pedantic quibbling about words … but appears to accept his responsibility in the matter.”
**Locus:** §36 Additional Notes, 4:27–28; slice ll. 123–125
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-08 — Gehazi’s failed staff-resurrection and Gospel echoes of need for the master’s presence
**Claim:** Gehazi gets “no sound or response” (echoing Carmel/Baal); only Elisha’s prayer and presence succeed. Provan notes Gospel parallels: disciples fail healing missions and need Jesus’ presence; highest faith trusts words alone (Luke 7:1–10), while resurrection stories pick up 2 Kgs 4 elements.
**Quote:** “Gehazi fails to evoke any response from the corpse (v. 31), just as those on Carmel had failed to draw a response from the ‘corpse’ of Baal … A number of Gospel passages seem to echo this story … They, like Gehazi, fail to fulfill their assigned tasks … and require Jesus’ own presence. … the highest commendation is reserved for those who believe that only his words are necessary (e.g., Luke 7:1–10).”
**Locus:** §36 + Additional Notes 4:29; slice ll. 89, 127
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[elijah]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-09 — Multiplied food: LORD heals and provides; Gospel feeding echoes
**Claim:** Poisoned stew and twenty-loaf multiplication conclude that the LORD heals and provides and that Elijah’s God is now Elisha’s; servant incomprehension and surplus anticipate Gospel feeding narratives.
**Quote:** “It is the chapter’s concluding demonstration that the LORD is a God who heals and provides; a God who brings life from death. It is also the final proof that the God of Elijah is now the God of Elisha. … We hear echoes of this story, of course, in the feeding narratives in the Gospels … in the face of incomprehension, food is multiplied to provide more than enough for all to eat.”
**Locus:** §36; 2 Kgs 4:38–44; slice ll. 91–93
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[elijah]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-10 — Naaman: LORD’s sovereignty over foreign success; only God kills and brings to life
**Claim:** Story opens by attributing Naaman’s military success to the LORD’s gift; Israel’s king is powerless before a demand proper only to God who “can kill and bring back to life,” recalling ch. 4 resurrection and exposing royal despair/ignorance of Elisha.
**Quote:** “The sovereignty of Israel’s God over the whole world is announced right at the beginning of the story, as we are told that—whatever Naaman himself may think—his success in life comes to him as the LORD’s gift (v. 1). … The king, of course, is powerless to help. It is an impossible demand for someone who is not God, for someone who cannot kill and bring back to life (v. 7 …). … But it also calls to mind that it is the LORD, and not the servant-prophet, who is in control of human destiny.”
**Locus:** §37; 2 Kgs 5:1–8; slice ll. 153
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-11 — Naaman expects prophet-as-healer; delayed Jordan cure proves living LORD, not magic hand
**Claim:** Great-man Naaman assumes prophets control their gift and will heal “on the spot”; intermediary message and Jordan command humiliate him. Delay is theologically necessary: healing at a distance from the prophet shows Elisha’s God is a living person, not a metaphor for prophetic powers; ambiguity would remain had Elisha waved a hand.
**Quote:** “To Naaman, the LORD is only a local deity at the beck and call of the prophet. It is the prophet who is the healer, not the god. … The way the cure has been wrought, however, has made it clear to him that Elisha’s god is not simply a convenient metaphor for unnatural prophetic powers but a living person. Healing has not come via a semi–magical wave of the prophetic hand (v. 11). It has been delivered by the living LORD, at a distance from the prophet. It is the directness of God’s action that has convinced Naaman of God’s reality …”
**Locus:** §37; 2 Kgs 5:9–15; slice ll. 155–157
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-12 — Humble servants persuade; “no God in all the world except in Israel”
**Claim:** Naaman’s servants, accustomed to humiliation, show more insight than the exalted man; after washing he confesses monotheism. Elisha refuses gifts so the living LORD, not the prophet, takes center stage; Naaman will worship only the LORD (altar of Israelite earth) while seeking pardon for unavoidable Rimmon court duties.
**Quote:** “Naaman’s servants, more accustomed to being treated in such humbling ways, prevail upon him to do as he has been told, and he is miraculously cured. The humble have once again exhibited more insight than the exalted … Now I know that there is no God in all the world except in Israel … He refuses to accept any gift; for that is to trade in Naaman’s old currency. It is the living LORD, and not Elisha, who must take center stage. … Elisha’s ‘Go in peace’ (2 Kgs. 5:19) suggests a broad interpretation of the LORD’s forgiveness. Naaman would find it even in the midst of sin, as he worshiped another god.”
**Locus:** §37 + Additional Notes 5:18; slice ll. 157–159, 195
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-13 — Gehazi cashes in on an act of God; insider judgment vs foreigner grace
**Claim:** Gehazi’s greed seeks profit from God’s act; disease transfers to him. He says “as the LORD lives” without faith (contrast Elisha’s “whom I serve”). Provan’s note: *ṣāraʿaṯ* signals uncleanness and judgment; Naaman is outsider (foreigner + leper) graced, Gehazi the insider judged—inclusiveness paralleled in Isa 56 and the NT, especially **Luke 4:27**.
**Quote:** “Gehazi has sought to cash in on an act of God … He utters words that imply belief but does not have faith (as the LORD lives, v. 20; contrast v. 16, with its significant addition ‘whom I serve’). … Naaman is one who is in every sense ‘outside the camp’—a foreigner and a leper as well. Yet God has been and will be gracious to him, and God’s judgment will fall on the ‘insider’ Gehazi … There is an inclusiveness here that is also found in Isa. 56:1–8 and throughout the NT. We may note in particular Luke 4:27, where Jesus provokes anger among his hearers by reminding them that, although there were many in Israel with ‘leprosy’ … only the foreigner Naaman was healed.”
**Locus:** §37; 5:20–27 + Additional Notes 5:1; slice ll. 161, 183
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R5-14 — Naaman’s conversion: “great man” becomes “little child”; washing as new life
**Claim:** Wordplay *naʿarâ qeṭannâ* / *naʿar qāṭōn*: the great man must become a little child under prophetic authority. Provan clusters NT conversion themes (new birth, little children, washing that cleanses); Naaman embodies new life, Gehazi the old who cries “LORD, LORD.”
**Quote:** “The ‘great man’ (v. 1) had a problem, to which the ‘young girl’ had the solution, but it involved Naaman becoming, like her, ‘a little child.’ He is transformed … into someone under prophetic authority, humbly acknowledging his new faith. … New birth is required to see the kingdom of God … which is inhabited by little children … and not by the great or the wealthy … The rite of passage into new life is a washing that makes one truly clean … Naaman embodies new life, and Gehazi embodies the old, crying ‘LORD, LORD’ (v. 20) while his actions reveal where his heart really lies …”
**Locus:** §37 Additional Notes 5:14; slice ll. 193
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-15 — “God saves” the trivial as well as the significant (axehead)
**Claim:** Floating axehead is interposed so readers do not forget Elisha’s ministry to the humble; “God saves” individual Israelites as well as Israel; purposes take in trivial and significant. Gilgal group; iron floats after wood is thrown in—amazing but unsurprising after resurrection.
**Quote:** “Lest we forget that Elisha’s ministry embraced the humble as well as the great … a short story about an iron tool is first interposed. ‘God saves’ individual Israelites as well as Israel. God’s purposes take in the ‘trivial’ as well as the ‘significant.’ … Elisha has experience in manipulating waters … and he is able to make the iron float … It is an amazing event, though not in the least surprising to those who have read of the raising of the dead …”
**Locus:** §38; 2 Kgs 6:1–7; slice ll. 219–221
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-16 — Heavenly horses around Elisha; Arameans blinded and feasted into peace
**Claim:** Aramean king cannot see what Elisha sees; servant’s eyes open to the LORD’s army surrounding Elisha on the city hill. Prophetic *sanwērîm* puts captors at the seer’s mercy; they are led to Samaria, sight restored, and—against Jehoram’s desire to kill—fed and released, producing a deeper peace than ch. 5’s truce.
**Quote:** “Arameans may surround the city … but Elisha himself is surrounded by the army of the LORD … Their blindness to the odds is quickly compounded by a blindness … which puts them entirely at the mercy of the seer they had come to capture. … After a great feast, they are accordingly sent home, and there is a peace between Aram and Israel that transcends the uneasy peace described in 5:1ff.”
**Locus:** §38; 2 Kgs 6:15–23; slice ll. 225
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-17 — Elisha helps Jehoram without changing judgment on him
**Claim:** Improved tone in 6:8–10 does not mean king–prophet reconciliation: Jehoram is respectful when things go well, murderous when bad; Elisha/authors have not revised the verdict that he is an idolater destined for ch. 9 judgment. Intervention is only because “it is not yet the end.”
**Quote:** “Jehoram is quite prepared throughout his story to treat prophets properly when things are going well (as here). He is not quite so ready to do so when things are going badly … There is no evidence, on the other hand, that Elisha, or the authors, have changed their views about Jehoram since 2 Kgs. 3. He is an idolater throughout his reign … destined for the final judgment that Elisha will initiate in 2 Kgs. 9:1ff. If Elisha intervenes to help him, it is not because anything has changed. It is only because God has ordained that it is not yet the end.”
**Locus:** §38 Additional Notes 6:9; slice ll. 247
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-18 — Siege of Samaria: only the LORD can save; Jehoram’s “faith” turns murderous
**Claim:** Cannibal crisis shows Jehoram powerless (*yšʿ*); he himself affirms only the LORD who provides grain/wine can save—ironically reminded by the prophet named “God saves.” After Ahab-like sackcloth he snaps into Jezebel-like oath to behead Elisha, again treating the prophet as master of destinies.
**Quote:** “Only the LORD who provides such things can save, as Jehoram himself affirms at the reminding of the prophet whose name embodies this truth (Hb. ʾelîšāʿ, ‘God saves’). The only proper response in the face of disaster . . . from the LORD is to wait for deliverance … the humility of his father gives way to the bloodthirstiness of his mother, as he takes her kind of oath on his lips (v. 31 …) and sends a man … to remove Elisha’s head … Does he too believe that prophets are in control of their own and others’ destinies …?”
**Locus:** §39; 2 Kgs 6:24–33; slice ll. 273
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-19 — Four lepers as humble channels of salvation; officer judged for mocking the word
**Claim:** Four lepers (wordplay with Egypt) drive Arameans away by supernatural deception with heavenly army sounds; they become channels of blessing. Skeptical officer sees but does not eat—salvation for people, judgment for the mocker. **Thesis:** “It is the humble—in this case the lepers—who are the channels of God’s blessing to Israel.”
**Quote:** “A leper had first brought the Arameans to Samaria during Jehoram’s reign (2 Kgs. 5:1–7), and four men with leprosy … now drive them away. … Supernaturally deceived … the Arameans flee … He has stood in the way of God’s salvation, as kings and their officials often do in these Elisha stories … It is the humble—in this case the lepers—who are the channels of God’s blessing to Israel.”
**Locus:** §39; 2 Kgs 7:3–20; slice ll. 279–283
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-20 — Miracle via four lepers, not heavenly “windows”
**Claim:** Officer’s taunt about *ʾarubbôt* (“windows/floodgates”) of heaven is answered ironically: the miracle comes not through heavenly windows but via four (*ʾarbāʿâ*) mundane lepers—humble means again.
**Quote:** “Ironically, the miracle does not come via ‘windows’ in the heavens (ʾarubbôt) but via four (Hb. ʾarbāʿâ) rather more mundane lepers.”
**Locus:** §39 Additional Notes 7:2; slice ll. 311
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-21 — Shunammite land restored: God looks after those who look after prophets
**Claim:** 8:1–6 completes 4:13’s offer: after Philistine sojourn someone (possibly Jehoram, Naboth-like land-grab) has taken her land; providentially Gehazi is narrating her story to the king, who restores house, land, and lost income. Provan cites Matt 10:40–42.
**Quote:** “Providentially, however, just at the moment she arrives at the royal court after seven long years to beg for her house and land, Gehazi is telling the king all about her. His words serve as the advocacy on her behalf that Elisha had had in mind in 4:13 … God looks after those who look after his prophets (Matt. 10:40–42).”
**Locus:** §40; 2 Kgs 8:1–6; slice ll. 339

### C-R5-22 — Hazael rises without Elijah’s anointing; Elijah not crucial to the plan
**Claim:** Elisha in Damascus announces Ben-Hadad’s death and Hazael’s brutal future reign; Elijah’s failure to anoint Hazael does not thwart the LORD—Hazael succeeds without Elijah. Foreign king consults the LORD where Ahaziah sought Baal-Zebub.
**Quote:** “Elijah’s failure to anoint Hazael will not thwart the LORD’s purposes after all (cf. 1 Kgs. 19:15–18). Elijah was not even crucial to God’s plans in this respect, for Hazael succeeds to the throne without his help. … There is evident irony in the fact that a foreign king knows well enough to consult the LORD (v. 8) in such circumstances, whereas the Israelite Ahaziah had sought the opinion of Baal-Zebub …”
**Locus:** §40; 2 Kgs 8:7–15; slice ll. 341
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-23 — Judean Jehoram/Ahaziah: Ahab-disease south; Davidic lamp still held, but tension rises
**Claim:** Judah’s Jehoram walks in ways of Israel/Ahab (Baal via Athaliah’s intermarriage); yet LORD unwilling to destroy Judah because of David’s lamp—punishment by rod, not rejection. Ahaziah’s one-year reign and co-timing with Israel’s last year raise fear that David’s house, mixed with Ahab’s, may be swept into coming judgment; answer deferred through chs. 9–10.
**Quote:** “Judah is in a very different position than is Israel, nevertheless. … God has promised David a lamp … In this context, it is no surprise to find that the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah because of Jehoram’s sins. … We anticipate that the Davidic promise will hold good for Jehoram’s son as well as for his father. … Is the house of David, mixed up with Ahab’s house through marriage, to be caught up in the coming judgment after all? Or will the promise to David hold? The answer is difficult to determine throughout 2 Kings 9–10 …”
**Locus:** §40; 2 Kgs 8:16–29; slice ll. 343–347
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-25 — Jehu anointed by Elisha’s agent; fulfills what Elijah left undone
**Claim:** Elijah failed to anoint Jehu; Elisha sends a subordinate for secret Saul-like anointing at Ramoth Gilead; companions eagerly proclaim him king—possibly army unrest at Jehoram’s military failure. Earthquake replaces God’s “quiet ways.”

**Claim:** Deaths at Naboth’s plot fulfill Elijah’s blood-prophecy (now including Naboth’s sons); Ahaziah, linked by marriage and religion, shares Ahab-pattern death—judgment exceeds expectations; wrong place + wrong gods.

### C-R5-27 — Jezebel’s end fulfills dogs-prophecy; *ḥēl/ḥēleq* textual tension noted
**Claim:** Jezebel as adorned prostitute/fertility patron dies by eunuchs’ hands on ground by palace; dogs fulfill 1 Kgs 21:23. Provan notes difficult *ḥēl* (wall) vs *ḥēleq* (plot) between 1 Kgs 21:23 and 2 Kgs 9:10, 36—possible both-and topography, not simple corruption.
**Quote:** “Most of Jezebel is gone. Prophecy has again been fulfilled; it is just as Elijah said (1 Kgs. 21:23; cf. 2 Kgs. 9:10). Yet the end of the chapter throws up a particularly difficult problem … The majority of Hebrew MSS at 1 Kings 21:23 have Elijah saying that Jezebel would be eaten by dogs ‘by the wall (Hb. ḥēl) of Jezreel.’ The MT at 2 Kings 9:36 … has her eaten on the plot of ground (Hb. ḥēleq) at Jezreel.”
**Locus:** §41; 2 Kgs 9:30–37; slice ll. 409–411
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-28 — No *šālôm* while Baal’s “prostitution” remains
**Claim:** Jehoram’s *hašālôm* (“Is everything all right?”) meets first negative answer in Kings: all cannot be well while Baal-worship (prostitution/witchcraft language) continues; house of Ahab must be removed for true well-being (*šillamtî* wordplay).
**Quote:** “All cannot truly be well in Israel while the worship of Baal continues, for all is not well between Israel and the LORD. Jehoram is thus the first character in Kings to receive a negative answer (mâ haššālôm) to this question (hašālôm); for it is his father’s house that must be removed if there truly to be ‘well-being’ in Israel …”
**Locus:** §41 Additional Notes 9:22; slice ll. 443
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R5-29 — Jehu’s purge of Ahab’s house and Baal is thorough; Davidic relatives unexpectedly drawn in

### C-R5-30 — Jehu incomplete purge: calves remain; yet “right” and fourth-generation promise
**Claim:** **Key thesis:** Jehu destroys Baal but does nothing about Jeroboam’s golden calves (10:29, 31). Surprisingly he is said to have done *yāšār* (“right”)—language otherwise reserved for David and non-idolatrous Judean kings—and receives a David-like dynastic promise to the fourth generation (not eternal). Eradication of Baal so significant that Jeroboam-sins “pale into insignificance” for the moment; right outweighs wrong.
**Quote:** “Jehu has decisively dealt with Baal-worship, and yet, it turns out, he does nothing at all about the worship of the golden calves (vv. 29, 31). It is somewhat surprising, then, to find him addressed in verse 30 as one who has done what is right in the eyes of the LORD … It is even more surprising to find Jehu receiving a David-like dynastic promise. His descendants will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. This is not the same thing as a promise of eternal dynasty. … Evidently the eradication of Baal-worship is so significant that, for the moment, participation in the sins of Jeroboam pales into insignificance. What Jehu has done that is right (v. 30) far outweighs what he continues to do that is wrong (vv. 29, 31).”

## Key theses (Provan, this slice)

1. **Humble channels of salvation:** Powerless figures (servants, maid, lepers, nurse) consistently mediate or receive God’s work; kings/officials are ignorant, arrogant, or obstructive (C-05, 12, 19, 20, 34).
2. **Naaman the foreigner:** Grace to the outsider/leper; monotheistic confession via delayed, non-magical cure; Luke 4:27 typology; Gehazi the judged insider (C-10–14, 42).
3. **Prophets as channels, not controllers:** Partial revelation (Moab; possibly Hazael oracle); incomplete Elisha knowledge; God not a vending machine (C-03, 07, 24).
4. **Jehu incomplete purge:** Thorough against Ahab and Baal; silent on golden calves; still called *yāšār* with fourth-generation promise because Baal’s eradication outweighs Jeroboam-sins for now (C-29–30).
5. **Athaliah vs Davidic survival:** Judean “Jezebel” nearly extinguishes royal seed; Joash in temple preserves lamp; covenant renewal; legitimacy vs non-reign of Athaliah; “David survives Jezebel” (C-23, 32–34).
6. **Elisha’s death and bones:** Era of “God saves” ends; corpse/*šlḵ* // exile/*šlḵ*; residual power and hope of resurrection if prophetic teaching retained (C-39).
7. **Abraham // David for the North:** 13:23 inserts everlasting patriarchal grace under northern law/exile trajectory; grace will triumph (C-37, 40).
8. **Compassion vs austerity / Elisha vs Elijah:** Double portion → denser provision/healing ministry for humble and foreigner, then completion of Elijah’s judgment via Jehu (C-06, 09, 41, 46).

## §46 Excursus summary (full)

Provan’s **“Elisha in Canonical Context”** places Elisha as **Joshua to Elijah’s Moses**: same life-from-death and foreigner-salvation patterns, greater miracle count after the double portion of spirit, and a dual name/role—**Elisha (“God saves”) son of Shaphat (“judgment”)**—so blessing and curse, salvation and judgment travel together. He can still mediate provisional salvation to Jehoram (as the unnamed prophet did for Ahab in 1 Kgs 20), but his destiny is to complete Elijah’s program in the destruction of Ahab’s house and the official end of Baal-worship.

**NT reception:** Named only in **Luke 4:27**, where Elisha/Naaman typologizes **Jesus’ Gentile mission**. Implicit Gospel parallels are many: leper healings; water transformation; gravity-defying water acts (axehead // sea-walking); raisings of the dead; food multiplications—especially for the humble; also curses, sight/blindness reversals, and kingdom justice.  

**Why underplayed:** Joshua and Elisha are both **successors** of more famous figures; given John-as-Elijah, the church avoided any Jesus-as-John’s-successor implication that would diminish Jesus’ pre-eminence (cf. John 1). Names Joshua/Elisha/Jesus share the “God saves” sense, which makes the silence more striking.  

**Exemplarity:** Solomon and Elijah are clearer NT models for believers; Elisha is less clear—possible in **Heb 11:34–35** (maybe 36)—while Acts shows the church mediating salvation *and* judgment in Elisha/Jesus fashion (Acts 5; 9).
